title: the Sri Sukta
hook: a cowshed at dawn, smoke and jasmine in the same breath, and a goddess whose doorway is fragrance

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta gave misfortune a face, Alakshmi, the elder one, and the singer helped show her the door. Which corner did you clear? Today, what the hymn counts as riches. Day one thousand ninety-eight.

A village before sunrise smells like several things at once. Woodsmoke. Wet earth. Milk warming in a pot. The cowshed, which nobody would call perfume. And then, from somewhere, a string of jasmine on a doorframe. Every one of those smells means the household is alive: there's fuel, there's food, there are animals fed, there's someone who cared enough to hang flowers. Today's lines of the Sri Sukta smell like that morning. They ask for riches, and the riches they name start in the cowshed and end in a person's mouth.
screen: `WOODSMOKE, WET EARTH, WARM MILK.` → `THE COWSHED, AND JASMINE.` → `A HOUSEHOLD THAT'S ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line, in paraphrase. Her doorway is fragrance. She is hard to overcome, always flourishing, rich in cow dung, the queen of all beings: I call Sri near. Yes, rich in cow dung. It's there in the Sanskrit, karishini, right next to queen of all beings, and the hymn sees no contradiction. In a farming household dung is fuel for the fire, food for the fields, and plaster for the floor. It means the cattle are healthy and the soil will feed you. So the goddess of fortune smells of jasmine at the door and of the cowshed out back, and both are signs of her. Now the next line, which goes somewhere else entirely. In paraphrase: may we gain the wish of the mind, the intention of the heart, the truth of speech. The beauty of cattle, and of food. May Sri and good name rest in me. Look at that list. Before it gets to cattle and food, it asks for things nobody can store in a barn. The mind's wish, fulfilled. An intention carried through. Truth in what you say. In the middle of a hymn about fortune, truth of speech is counted as riches. Some readers hear the two lines as a pair. One is the outer household: animals, fuel, fields, a fragrant door. The other is the inner one: a clear mind, a kept intention, honest words. And the hymn asks that Sri rest in the person, not only in the barn. Others simply hear a full life, described from the ground up. Either way, the fortune this hymn wants is wider than money, and earthier, and it includes the way a person talks.
screen: `HER DOORWAY IS FRAGRANCE.` · `RICH IN COW DUNG, QUEEN OF ALL.` · `THE WISH, THE INTENTION, THE TRUTH.` · `MAY SRI REST IN ME.` · then, large: `TRUTH OF SPEECH, COUNTED AS RICHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take inventory, both kinds. Settle, and let the breath slow. First, notice the earthy riches around you right now: the air, a roof, water within reach, food somewhere in the kitchen. Name them quietly, one per breath. Then turn inward. Is there one intention you've been carrying? One thing you said this week that was simply true? Let that count too. Breathe with both lists for a while. If you pray, you can give thanks to the goddess, or to God, for them in your own words. If you don't, just let yourself be a little richer than you thought. The bell holds the time.
The Sri Sukta. A hymn that calls Sri fragrant at the door and rich in cow dung, and asks for truth of speech in the same breath as cattle and food.
Your line: the Sri Sukta. Today, count one honest sentence as part of your wealth: say something true that you'd been rounding off. Day one thousand ninety-eight.

howItsDone: In some Hindu homes, especially in villages, cattle are honored at festivals and floors and courtyards are freshly plastered and decorated before Lakshmi worship; the Sri Sukta is chanted as part of that worship.

fork.setup: you're listing the riches you'd like the goddess to bring. after the mind's wish and the heart's intention, what comes next?
fork.reveal: the hymn asks for truth of speech, and only then for the beauty of cattle and food. honest words are counted among the riches.

original.note: Sanskrit: karīṣiṇīm, 'rich in cow dung,' a name for Sri in the Sri Sukta, beside 'queen of all beings'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a goddess of wealth is all gold and jewels.
what it means: the hymn calls her fragrant and rich in cow dung, and asks for truth of speech among the riches.
what a scholar hears: gandhadvārāṃ ... karīṣiṇīm / īśvarīṃ sarvabhūtānām, then vācaḥ satyam aśīmahi: the farmyard and the honest tongue in neighboring lines.

sources.ref: Sri Sukta, verses 9–10 (Rig Veda khila, as commonly recited)

notes: Verse 9 paraphrased: gandhadvārāṃ durādharṣāṃ nityapuṣṭāṃ karīṣiṇīm / īśvarīṃ sarvabhūtānāṃ tām ihopahvaye śriyam. karīṣiṇī glossed 'rich in cow dung' (karīṣa, dried dung); some translators soften it to 'abounding in cattle wealth'. Confirm the plain rendering is acceptable for this audience.
Verse 10 paraphrased: manasaḥ kāmam ākūtiṃ vācaḥ satyam aśīmahi / paśūnāṃ rūpam annasya mayi śrīḥ śrayatāṃ yaśaḥ. ākūti glossed 'intention of the heart'; yaśas as 'good name'. Confirm.
Uses of dung (fuel, fertilizer, floor plaster) are given as everyday rural practice, not tied to the text; confirm.
The two readings (outer and inner household; a full life described from the ground up) are offered without ranking.
